claim: Aneuploidy in human eggs is the leading cause of pregnancy loss and Down's syndrome.
source: Aneuploidy in human eggs is the leading cause of pregnancy loss and Down's syndrome.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the consequences of aneuploidy in human eggs.

claim: Aneuploid eggs result from chromosome segregation errors when an egg develops from a progenitor cell, called an oocyte.
source: Aneuploid eggs result from chromosome segregation errors when an egg develops from a progenitor cell, called an oocyte.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the origin of aneuploid eggs.

claim: 60% of sister kinetochores in human oocytes from young women (≤30 years) appeared as two discrete spots when observed by light microscopy.
source: Unexpectedly, 60% of sister kinetochores appeared as two discrete spots when observed by light microscopy (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of 1,051 chromosomes from 23 oocytes, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Sister kinetochores in oocytes from young mice generally appear as a single spot.
source: This is in contrast to oocytes from young mice, whose sister kinetochores generally appear as a single spot (Chiang et al., 2010, Lister et al., 2010, Shomper et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on mouse oocytes.

claim: Sister kinetochores in human oocytes were spaced up to 1.7 µm apart.
source: The sister kinetochores were spaced up to 1.7 µm apart (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by distance measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Around 90% of split kinetochores were attached to two separate kinetochore fibers.
source: Around 90% of split kinetochores were attached to two separate kinetochore fibers (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of 949 attachments from 25 cold-treated human oocytes, as shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The fraction of split kinetochores in human oocytes increased with maternal age.
source: The fraction of split kinetochores in human oocytes increased with maternal age.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D-E comparing different age groups.

claim: Around 75% of all kinetochores were split in oocytes from women between 30 and 35.
source: Around 75% of all kinetochores were split in oocytes from women between 30 and 35.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 87% of kinetochores were split in women over 35.
source: This increased to 87% in women over 35 (Figure 2A–E; Videos 1, 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Separated sister kinetochores were more likely to be merotelically attached to the spindle than unified sister kinetochores.
source: Separated sister kinetochores were more likely to be merotelically attached to the spindle than unified sister kinetochores.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The fraction of merotelic attachments increased from 12% in unified kinetochore pairs to 17% when the sister kinetochores were distinct but still linked, and up to 28% in completely separated kinetochore pairs.
source: the fraction of merotelic attachments increased from 12% in unified kinetochore pairs to 17% when the sister kinetochores were distinct but still linked, and up to 28% in completely separated kinetochore pairs (Figure 2F,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The number of merotelic kinetochore-microtubule attachments increased with maternal age, from around 7% in women under 30 to around 21% in women over 35.
source: The number of merotelic kinetochore-microtubule attachments also increased with maternal age, from around 7% in women under 30 to around 21% in women over 35 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: A large fraction of oocytes had one or more rotated bivalent chromosomes, in which the sister kinetochores of both pairs faced opposite spindle poles.
source: To our surprise, a large fraction of oocytes had one or more rotated bivalent chromosomes, in which the sister kinetochores of both pairs faced opposite spindle poles (Figure 3A–C, middle row; Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Videos 5, 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: More than 2% of all bivalents were half or fully inverted.
source: In total, more than 2% of all bivalents were half or fully inverted (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The incidence of inverted bivalents increased with maternal age, from 12.5% in oocytes from women under 30 to 40% in oocytes from women over 35 years old.
source: Moreover, the incidence of inverted bivalents increased with maternal age, from 12.5% in oocytes from women under 30 to 40% in oocytes from women over 35 years old (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In around 20% of bivalents with split sister kinetochores, the chromosomes were twisted.
source: In around 20% of bivalents with split sister kinetochores, the chromosomes were twisted, as judged by the observation that their sister kinetochore pairs were oriented perpendicular instead of parallel to each other (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 10% of all bivalents were weakly associated as evident from a gap in the bivalents' center.
source: In total, 10% of all bivalents were weakly associated as evident from a gap in the bivalents' center.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 1.2% of bivalents completely disintegrated into univalents.
source: Insufficient arm cohesion was also evident from the complete disintegration of 1.2% of bivalents into univalents (Figure 5B–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 95% of univalents aligned in the center of the spindle, with their sister kinetochores facing opposite spindle poles.
source: 95% of these univalents aligned in the center of the spindle, with their sister kinetochores facing opposite spindle poles, suggesting that they could segregate equally into two sister chromatids upon anaphase onset (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In women under 30, 5% of all chromosome pairs were separated by gaps or completely disintegrated into univalents.
source: In women under 30, 5% of all chromosome pairs were separated by gaps or completely disintegrated into univalents.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 11% of chromosome pairs in women over 35 years old were separated by gaps or completely disintegrated into univalents.
source: This increased to 11% of chromosome pairs in women over 35 years old (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: More than 40% of oocytes from women over 35 featured univalents.
source: However, it is unclear whether mechanisms exist in the oocyte that could detect these inverted bivalents and correct their attachment. Our observation that human oocytes progress into anaphase efficiently even if misaligned chromosomes are present suggests that oocytes could in principle also progress into anaphase with inverted bivalents (Figure 7). Such inverted bivalents could lag behind during anaphase if centromeric cohesion is still intact in one or both of the two pairs of sister kinetochores.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Around 16.3 ± 2.3 hr were needed to align the chromosomes in the center of the spindle upon nuclear envelope breakdown.
source: Live imaging in human oocytes showed that around 16.3 ± 2.3 hr were needed to align the chromosomes in the center of the spindle upon nuclear envelope breakdown (Holubcova et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: All oocytes without chromosome alignment defects progressed into anaphase.
source: Live imaging revealed that all oocytes without chromosome alignment defects progressed into anaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: All oocytes with mild alignment defects progressed into anaphase.
source: Similarly, all oocytes with mild alignment defects and 92% of oocytes with severe misalignment progressed into anaphase (Figure 6A,B; Videos 7, 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 92% of oocytes with severe misalignment progressed into anaphase.
source: Similarly, all oocytes with mild alignment defects and 92% of oocytes with severe misalignment progressed into anaphase (Figure 6A,B; Videos 7, 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The onset of anaphase was not severely delayed when misaligned or lagging chromosomes were present.
source: In addition, the onset of anaphase was not severely delayed when misaligned or lagging chromosomes were present (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by timing analysis shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Human oocytes segregate their chromosomes much more inaccurately than do human mitotic cells.
source: Surprisingly, oocytes segregate their chromosomes much more inaccurately than do human mitotic cells (Nagaoka et al., 2012, Knouse et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human oocytes segregate their chromosomes much more inaccurately than human spermatocytes.
source: Surprisingly, oocytes segregate their chromosomes much more inaccurately than do human mitotic cells (Nagaoka et al., 2012, Knouse et al., 2014), human spermatocytes (Pacchierotti et al., 2007, Templado et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human oocytes segregate their chromosomes much more inaccurately than mouse oocytes.
source: Surprisingly, oocytes segregate their chromosomes much more inaccurately than do human mitotic cells (Nagaoka et al., 2012, Knouse et al., 2014), human spermatocytes (Pacchierotti et al., 2007, Templado et al., 2011) or mouse oocytes (Pacchierotti et al., 2007, Danylevska et al., 2014, Hassold and Hunt, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The accuracy of chromosome segregation drops with increasing age.
source: The accuracy of chromosome segregation drops even further with increasing age (Nagaoka et al., 2012, Chiang et al., 2010, Fragouli et al., 2011, Kuliev et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Eggs from young women are also often aneuploid.
source: Notably, eggs from young women are also often aneuploid (Pacchierotti et al., 2007, Obradors et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human oocytes assemble a spindle by an unusually long and error-prone mechanism.
source: We showed previously that human oocytes assemble a spindle by an unusually long and error-prone mechanism that is likely to sensitize human oocytes of all ages to abnormal kinetochore-microtubule attachments and chromosome segregation errors (Holubcova et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Changes in chromosome architecture contribute to the age-dependent increase in aneuploidy in mouse oocytes.
source: Research in mouse oocytes suggests that changes in chromosome architecture contribute to this age-dependent increase in aneuploidy (Lister et al., 2010, Chiang et al., 2011, Yun et al., 2014, Sakakibara et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in mouse oocytes.

claim: During the first meiotic division, the oocyte segregates entire chromosomes instead of sister chromatids as is the case in mitosis.
source: During the first meiotic division, the oocyte segregates entire chromosomes instead of sister chromatids as is the case in mitosis.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about meiosis I.

claim: Chromosome pairs are linked with each other through meiotic recombination.
source: To facilitate this, the chromosome pairs are linked with each other through meiotic recombination (Nagaoka et al., 2012, Kong et al., 2004, Baudat et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The sister kinetochores of each chromosome become unified so that they function as a single kinetochore during meiosis I.
source: The sister kinetochores of each chromosome become unified so that they function as a single kinetochore (Watanabe, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Unified sister kinetochores prevent the undesirable bi-orientation of sister kinetochores during meiosis I.
source: This prevents the undesirable bi-orientation of sister kinetochores during meiosis I (Watanabe, 2012, Yokobayashi and Watanabe, 2005, Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cohesion complex holds the homologous chromosomes together.
source: The cohesion complex has a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the bivalents: it holds the homologous chromosomes together and promotes the close association of the sister kinetochores (Petronczki et al., 2003, Watanabe, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cohesion complex promotes the close association of the sister kinetochores.
source: The cohesion complex has a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the bivalents: it holds the homologous chromosomes together and promotes the close association of the sister kinetochores (Petronczki et al., 2003, Watanabe, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cohesin complex is gradually lost from oocyte chromosomes as mice get older.
source: Recent work in mouse oocytes suggests that the cohesin complex is gradually lost from oocyte chromosomes as mice get older (Lister et al., 2010, Tachibana-Konwalski et al., 2010, Chiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in mouse oocytes.

claim: Loss of cohesin leads to an increase in sister kinetochore distances in mouse oocytes.
source: This loss of cohesin has been suggested to lead to an increase in sister kinetochore distances and the precocious dissociation of bivalents into individual chromosomes (Yun et al., 2014, Sakakibara et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in mouse oocytes.

claim: Loss of cohesin leads to the precocious dissociation of bivalents into individual chromosomes in mouse oocytes.
source: This loss of cohesin has been suggested to lead to an increase in sister kinetochore distances and the precocious dissociation of bivalents into individual chromosomes (Yun et al., 2014, Sakakibara et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in mouse oocytes.

claim: The study analyzed the organization of chromosomes and how they interact with the spindle in over 200 live and fixed human oocytes from donors aged between 23 and 46 years.
source: To this end, we analyzed the organization of chromosomes and how they interact with the spindle in over 200 live and fixed human oocytes from donors aged between 23 and 46 years.
evidence: This describes the methodology and sample size of the study.

claim: High resolution z-stacks of 1,051 chromosomes and their kinetochores in 23 oocytes from young women (≤30 years) were recorded.
source: We first investigated the chromosome organization in oocytes from young women (≤30 years) by recording high resolution z-stacks (300 nm in x and y, 650 nm in z) of 1,051 chromosomes and their kinetochores in 23 oocytes.
evidence: This describes the methodology and sample size for the initial analysis.

claim: Bivalents with separated kinetochores were observed throughout the entire cohort of oocyte donors.
source: Such bivalents with separated kinetochores were a frequent phenomenon, observed throughout the entire cohort of oocyte donors (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1,2), including very young donors (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations across all age groups shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: The two kinetochore fibers of split kinetochores did not always run in parallel, but often linked the sister kinetochores to distant positions at the spindle poles.
source: The two kinetochore fibers did not always run in parallel, but often linked the sister kinetochores to distant positions at the spindle poles (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1D,F.

claim: The spindle recognizes most split sister kinetochores in human oocytes as independent units.
source: Thus, consistent with the high degree of separation, the spindle recognizes most split sister kinetochores in human oocytes as independent units (Figure 1—figure supplement 3,4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that split kinetochores attach to separate k-fibers.

claim: Sister kinetochores in mouse oocytes sometimes become distinguishable in oocytes from very old mice.
source: Sister kinetochores also sometimes become distinguishable in oocytes from very old mice (Chiang et al., 2010, Lister et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in mouse oocytes.

claim: In contrast to human oocytes, sister kinetochores in mouse oocytes are not separated by a prominent gap.
source: But in contrast to human oocytes, their sister kinetochores are not separated by a prominent gap.
evidence: This is a comparison between human and mouse oocytes based on the authors' observations and previous literature.

claim: Sister kinetochores were separated by very large gaps during meiosis II in human oocytes.
source: Consistent with the remarkably large distances between sister kinetochores during meiosis I (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and meiosis II (Duncan et al., 2012) in human oocytes, sister kinetochores were also separated by very large gaps during meiosis II (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Videos 3, 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of bivalent chromosomes in human oocytes feature three or four functionally distinct kinetochores.
source: Together, these data show that the majority of bivalent chromosomes in human oocytes feature three or four functionally distinct kinetochores.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the observation that most sister kinetochores are split and attach to separate k-fibers.

claim: Each of the functionally distinct kinetochores on bivalent chromosomes is able to establish its own kinetochore fiber.
source: Each of these kinetochores is able to establish its own kinetochore fiber.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that split kinetochores attach to separate k-fibers.

claim: Human oocytes question the paradigm that sister kinetochores are unified during meiosis I.
source: Thus, human oocytes question the paradigm that sister kinetochores are unified during meiosis I.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the observation that most sister kinetochores in human oocytes are split.

claim: During meiosis I, the sister kinetochores of each chromosome should be attached to a single spindle pole only (amphitelic attachment).
source: During meiosis I, the sister kinetochores of each chromosome should be attached to a single spindle pole only (amphitelic attachment).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about correct kinetochore attachment in meiosis I.

claim: If a pair of sister kinetochores is attached to opposite spindle poles (merotelic attachment), the chromosome will be pulled from both sides of the spindle upon anaphase onset.
source: If a pair of sister kinetochores is attached to opposite spindle poles instead (merotelic attachment), the chromosome will be pulled from both sides of the spindle upon anaphase onset.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the consequences of merotelic attachments.

claim: Merotelic attachments can lead to aneuploidy when the ingressing cytokinetic furrow partitions chromosomes inaccurately between the egg and the polar body.
source: This can lead to aneuploidy when the ingressing cytokinetic furrow partitions chromosomes inaccurately between the egg and the polar body.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about the consequences of chromosome lagging during anaphase.

claim: Cold treatment selectively preserves the more stable microtubules that interact with kinetochores.
source: This selectively preserves the more stable microtubules that interact with kinetochores (Zhai et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The degree of separation between sister kinetochores correlated with the probability of a pair being merotelically attached.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the degree of separation correlated with the probability of a pair being merotelically attached
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Improved accessibility from the opposite spindle pole could explain why separated kinetochores are more likely to be merotelically attached.
source: This could potentially be due to improved accessibility from the opposite spindle pole, when two tightly joined sister kinetochores are compared with two separated sister kinetochores.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed correlation between separation and merotelic attachments.

claim: Separated kinetochores were more likely to be merotelically attached in oocytes from older women than in oocytes from young women.
source: Separated kinetochores were more likely to be merotelically attached in oocytes from older women than in oocytes from young women (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The increase in merotelic attachments with age could be explained by the increase in the degree of separation between sister kinetochores as women get older.
source: This could be explained by the increase in the degree of separation between sister kinetochores as women get older (Figure 2C), as well as additional age-related defects that could contribute to aberrant attachments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between separation and merotelic attachments.

claim: A stable arrangement of bivalent chromosomes on the spindle could theoretically be achieved if the split sister kinetochores are facing towards opposite poles instead of the same spindle pole.
source: The remarkably large distances between some sister kinetochores raised an unexpected problem: a stable arrangement of bivalent chromosomes on the spindle could theoretically also be achieved if the split sister kinetochores are facing towards opposite poles instead of the same spindle pole (Figure 3A scheme, middle row; fully-rotated).
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration based on the observation of large distances between sister kinetochores.

claim: A chromosome rotated by 90 degrees on the spindle could not segregate accurately during anaphase.
source: Such a chromosome would be rotated on the spindle by 90 degrees and could not segregate accurately during anaphase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expected behavior of rotated bivalents during anaphase.

claim: Kinetochores of inverted bivalents were linked to the spindle through cold-resistant and thus stable microtubules.
source: Importantly, kinetochores of inverted bivalents were linked to the spindle through cold-resistant and thus stable microtubules (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: The altered orientation of kinetochores in inverted bivalents does not completely compromise their ability to capture microtubules.
source: This indicates that the altered orientation of kinetochores in inverted bivalents does not completely compromise their ability to capture microtubules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that inverted bivalents have stable microtubule attachments.

claim: The increased separation of sister kinetochores with maternal age is expected to promote bivalent rotation.
source: This is consistent with the increased separation of sister kinetochores with maternal age, which is expected to promote the rotation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between separation and rotation.

claim: In around 20% of bivalents with split sister kinetochores, the chromosomes were twisted.
source: In around 20% of bivalents with split sister kinetochores, the chromosomes were twisted, as judged by the observation that their sister kinetochore pairs were oriented perpendicular instead of parallel to each other (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Twisting is likely to exert additional forces on arm cohesion.
source: Such twisting is likely to exert additional forces on arm cohesion, which is possibly already weakened in oocytes at the time of meiotic resumption (Duncan et al., 2012, Chiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expected mechanical consequences of twisting.

claim: Arm cohesion is possibly already weakened in oocytes at the time of meiotic resumption.
source: Such twisting is likely to exert additional forces on arm cohesion, which is possibly already weakened in oocytes at the time of meiotic resumption (Duncan et al., 2012, Chiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Arm cohesion was reduced in a large fraction of chromosome bivalents.
source: Arm cohesion was indeed reduced in a large fraction of chromosome bivalents (Figure 5A,C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5A,C,D.

claim: Gaps between two chromosomes of up to 3.2 µm were visible in some bivalents.
source: In other cases, gaps of up to 3.2 µm between two chromosomes were visible (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Chromosomes with reduced arm cohesion still behave as functional bivalents.
source: This suggests that chromosomes with reduced arm cohesion still behave as functional bivalents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that chromosomes with gaps are still under tension.

claim: The premature dissociation of bivalents into univalents contributes to aneuploidy in oocytes from young women.
source: Our data suggests that the premature dissociation of bivalents into univalents also contributes to aneuploidy in oocytes from young women (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of univalents in oocytes from young women.

claim: An increase in univalents is a likely contributor to the maternal age effect.
source: It also provides further evidence from a larger number of oocytes that an increase in univalents is a likely contributor to the maternal age effect, because more than 40% of oocytes from women over 35 featured univalents (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased frequency of univalents with age.

claim: Having more than two functional kinetochores on each bivalent chromosome is expected to hinder the correct attachment of chromosomes to the spindle.
source: Having more than two functional kinetochores on each bivalent chromosome is expected to hinder the correct attachment of chromosomes to the spindle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased complexity of attachment with more kinetochores.

claim: The period of chromosome congression and alignment coincided in time with spindle instability and reorganization.
source: The period of chromosome congression and alignment coincided in time with spindle instability and reorganization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reorganization of the spindle is required to attach the bivalent chromosomes correctly to the spindle.
source: It is conceivable that the reorganization of the spindle is required to attach the bivalent chromosomes correctly to the spindle, consistent with a previous study in mouse oocytes (Kitajima et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation to a previous study in mouse oocytes.

claim: Difficulties in correctly attaching bivalents to the spindle would only lead to aneuploidy if oocytes are allowed to progress into anaphase in the presence of abnormal kinetochore-microtubule attachments.
source: Difficulties in correctly attaching bivalents to the spindle would only lead to aneuploidy if oocytes are allowed to progress into anaphase in the presence of abnormal kinetochore-microtubule attachments.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the conditions necessary for aneuploidy to result from attachment errors.

claim: The spindle assembly checkpoint delays progression into anaphase until all chromosomes are correctly attached to the spindle in mitosis.
source: In mitosis, the spindle assembly checkpoint delays progression into anaphase until all chromosomes are correctly attached to the spindle (Musacchio and Salmon, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The presence of chromosome alignment defects did not preclude progression into anaphase in human oocytes.
source: Thus, the presence of chromosome alignment defects did not preclude progression into anaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Human oocytes progress into anaphase with normal efficiency and without major delays if chromosomes are misaligned.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that human oocytes progress into anaphase with normal efficiency and without major delays if chromosomes are misaligned.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the timing and efficiency data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Merotelic attachments are promoted by the high instability and morphology of the spindle in human oocytes.
source: These merotelic attachments could be favoured by the high instability and morphology of the spindle in human oocytes (Holubcova et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The fact that the four sister kinetochores of a bivalent chromosome can interact with microtubules independently may make it more challenging for the oocyte to correctly attach the bivalents to the spindle.
source: It is conceivable that the specialized architecture of bivalents in human oocytes and spindle reorganization are directly linked: the fact that the four sister kinetochores of a bivalent chromosome can interact with microtubules independently may make it more challenging for the oocyte to correctly attach the bivalents to the spindle.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed spindle reorganization.

claim: More extensive spindle reorganization may be required to correct attachment errors that arise during spindle assembly.
source: Thus, more extensive spindle reorganization may be required to correct attachment errors that arise during spindle assembly.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed spindle reorganization.

claim: Repeated rounds of microtubule attachment and detachment during spindle reorganization may exacerbate splitting of sister kinetochores.
source: Conversely, repeated rounds of microtubule attachment and detachment during spindle reorganization may further exacerbate splitting of sister kinetochores and cause strain on chromosome arm cohesion, promoting the twisting of bivalents and the precocious dissociation of bivalents into univalents.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed chromosome defects.

claim: Spindle reorganization could contribute to chromosome segregation defects in human oocytes.
source: In this way, spindle reorganization could contribute to chromosome segregation defects in human oocytes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the proposed mechanisms.

claim: Bivalents disintegrate precociously into univalents as women get older.
source: We show that bivalents disintegrate precociously into univalents as women get older.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5D,F.

claim: Univalents are a major contributor to the maternal age effect.
source: Univalents were observed in more than 40% of oocytes from women over 35, suggesting that they are a major contributor to the maternal age effect, consistent with a recent study (Sakakibara et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the high frequency of univalents in older women, supported by a citation.

claim: The degree of sister kinetochore separation increases with advanced maternal age.
source: We also demonstrate that the degree of sister kinetochore separation increases with advanced maternal age.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Sister kinetochore separation correlated with merotelic kinetochore-microtubule attachment.
source: Sister kinetochore separation correlated with merotelic kinetochore-microtubule attachment.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Sister kinetochore separation allowed bivalents to rotate on the spindle with each of their sister-kinetochores facing towards opposite spindle poles.
source: In addition, it allowed bivalents to rotate on the spindle with each of their sister-kinetochores facing towards opposite spindle poles.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: It is generally believed that mechanisms exist that prevent the biorientation of sister kinetochores in meiosis I.
source: This is unexpected, because it is generally believed that mechanisms exist that prevent the biorientation of sister kinetochores in meiosis I.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Half- or fully-inverted bivalents were observed in a large fraction of oocytes.
source: We observed half- or fully-inverted bivalents in a large fraction of oocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Some inverted bivalents may be corrected by the time of anaphase onset.
source: It is possible that some of these abnormal attachments are corrected by the time of anaphase onset.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the fate of inverted bivalents.

claim: It is unclear whether mechanisms exist in the oocyte that could detect inverted bivalents and correct their attachment.
source: However, it is unclear whether mechanisms exist in the oocyte that could detect these inverted bivalents and correct their attachment.
evidence: This is a statement about the uncertainty regarding correction mechanisms.

claim: Human oocytes could progress into anaphase with inverted bivalents.
source: Our observation that human oocytes progress into anaphase efficiently even if misaligned chromosomes are present suggests that oocytes could in principle also progress into anaphase with inverted bivalents (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that oocytes progress into anaphase with misaligned chromosomes.

claim: Inverted bivalents could lag behind during anaphase if centromeric cohesion is still intact in one or both of the two pairs of sister kinetochores.
